summary: Small carpetgrass is a low, sprawling annual grass that grows up to about a foot and a half tall. Its stems root where they touch the ground, and its short, broad, bright green leaves (up to about 3 inches long) wrap around the stem. It grows fast and competes very well in moist soil, where it can form dense stands that crowd out native plants and may change which plants grow there. It does best in moist, sunny places such as stream banks, the edges of ponds and lakes, wet meadows and other open, damp, disturbed ground.
history: Small carpetgrass is native to Asia (NYIS lists eastern Asia including India, New Guinea and Japan, plus Australia). No one knows exactly when or how it reached North America, but its patchy spread suggests it arrived by accident several times, perhaps as early as the late 1800s. It now grows in at least 25 states.
seasons: It is an annual, so each plant lives for one year and makes a lot of seed. Its flowers appear toward the end of summer, in a cluster of up to 10 finger-like spikes that can be greenish to purple.

handling.text: Hand pulling works if it is done before the plant makes seed, and mowing or cutting works if it is started when the plant begins to flower, not earlier. Larger patches may also need herbicide. Because new seedlings can come up, treated spots should be checked again for at least a year. Seeds spread by wind, water and people, including on clothing and in moved soil.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
